question_text: A 35-year-old man is brought to the emergency department because of a 2-week history of abdominal cramps, vomiting, and constipation. He also reports having to urinate frequently and occasional leg pain. He has had similar episodes in the past. He has hypertension and peptic ulcer disease. Current medications include captopril and ranitidine. He appears depressed. Physical examination shows weakness in the extremities. Abdominal examination shows mild epigastric tenderness. There is no rebound or guarding. He has a restricted affect. Laboratory studies show elevated serum parathyroid hormone levels; serum calcium is 14.2 mg/dL. Abdominal ultrasonography shows multiple small calculi in the right kidney. Which of the following is most likely to provide rapid relief in this patient?

The most effective and rapid treatment for hypercalcemia involves the use of normal saline and intravenous furosemide therapy, which promotes renal excretion of calcium, thereby reducing serum calcium levels and alleviating symptoms. This approach is supported by the consensus that hydration with normal saline and the use of diuretics like furosemide are standard treatments for acute hypercalcemia. Other options, such as intravenous pamidronate or calcitonin, are not as immediate in providing symptom relief compared to the combination of normal saline and furosemide.
